Measures of relatedness

Source: R/metrics.R
relatedness_metrics.Rd

fastrel_ped(), fastrel_vec() and rel_get() can return four measures of the genetic resemblance between individuals, chosen with their argument metric. All four are derived from the same quantity, the kinship coefficient, so choosing one or the other costs a single pass over the matrix at most.

metricMeasureFormula
"additive" (default)additive relationship\(A_{ij} = 2\phi_{ij}\)
"kinship"kinship coefficient\(\phi_{ij}\)
"wright"Wright's coefficient of relationship\(A_{ij} / \sqrt{A_{ii} A_{jj}}\)
"hamilton"Hamilton's coefficient of relatedness\(A_{ij} / A_{ii}\)

Their values are as follows:

metricDiagonalRange of the diagonalRange off the diagonalSymmetric
"additive"\(1 + F_i\)1 to 20 to 2yes
"kinship"\((1 + F_i)/2\)0.5 to 10 to 1yes
"wright"110 to 1yes
"hamilton"110 to 1no

Here \(\phi_{ij}\) is the kinship coefficient between individuals \(i\) and \(j\), and \(F_i\) is the inbreeding coefficient of \(i\). Without inbreeding (all \(F = 0\)) the measures "additive", "wright" and "hamilton" are identical, and equal twice the kinship coefficient: 0.5 for parent and offspring or full siblings, 0.25 for half siblings, 0.125 for first cousins. They differ only with inbreeding.

Kinship coefficient ("kinship")

The kinship coefficient \(\phi_{ij}\) (Malécot 1948, who called it the coefficient de parenté; it is also known as the coefficient of coancestry) is the probability that an allele drawn at random from \(i\) and an allele drawn at random from \(j\), at the same autosomal locus, are identical by descent, i.e. copies of a single allele of a common ancestor. Being a probability, it lies between 0 and 1. This is what kinship2::kinship() returns (Sinnwell et al. 2014).

Two related quantities follow. The inbreeding coefficient \(F_i\), introduced by Wright (1922) as the correlation between the egg and the sperm that unite to form \(i\), is the probability that the two alleles of \(i\) are identical by descent: Malécot (1948) defined it so, as his coefficient de consanguinité, and noted that it equals the kinship coefficient between the parents of \(i\). The kinship of an individual with itself is \(\phi_{ii} = (1 + F_i)/2\): when two alleles are drawn from \(i\) with replacement, the same allele is drawn twice with probability 1/2, and otherwise the two alleles are identical by descent with probability \(F_i\).

Additive relationship ("additive")

The additive relationship \(A_{ij} = 2\phi_{ij}\) is what animal and plant breeders call the numerator relationship, as it is the numerator of Wright's coefficient of relationship (see below). Emik and Terrill (1949) introduced this name and described the tabular method used here to compute it. Individuals are added one by one, parents before offspring. When individual \(i\), with mother \(m\) and father \(d\), is added:

  • its additive relationship with each individual \(j\) already present is the average of those of its two parents with \(j\), \(A_{ij} = (A_{mj} + A_{dj}) / 2\) (an unknown parent counting as 0);

  • its additive relationship with itself is \(A_{ii} = 1 + A_{md} / 2\), where \(A_{md}\) is the additive relationship between its two parents, since its inbreeding coefficient is half of that; if a parent is unknown, \(A_{ii} = 1\).

Henderson (1976) gives the same method for the whole numerator relationship matrix, as used to predict breeding values.

The additive relationship is not a probability but an expected count: \(A_{ij}\) is the expected number of the two alleles of \(j\) that are identical by descent with an allele drawn at random from \(i\), which is why it can exceed 1 (see the section Range of values). For example, two offspring obtained by selfing an individual that was itself obtained by selfing have an additive relationship of 1.5 (and a kinship of 0.75).

Its main use is quantitative genetics: under an additive model, the covariance between the breeding values of \(i\) and \(j\) is \(A_{ij} \sigma^2_A\), where \(\sigma^2_A\) is the additive genetic variance of the base population: the variance matrix of breeding values is \(A \sigma^2_A\) (Henderson 1976; Lynch and Walsh 1998, chapter 7). In a population without inbreeding, the covariance is thus half the additive variance between parent and offspring and a quarter of it between half siblings, as Falconer (1960, chapter 9) derives directly. The diagonal, \(1 + F_i\), shows that the breeding values of inbred individuals vary more, since inbred individuals are more homozygous. This matrix is the one used in animal models and to estimate heritability.

Wright's coefficient of relationship ("wright")

Wright (1922) defined the coefficient of relationship as the correlation between two individuals, i.e. between their genotypes (Michod and Hamilton 1980), which is obtained by dividing the covariance \(A_{ij}\) by the product of the two standard deviations, as in Wright's own formula: $$r_{ij} = \frac{A_{ij}}{\sqrt{A_{ii} A_{jj}}} = \frac{2\phi_{ij}}{\sqrt{(1 + F_i)(1 + F_j)}}$$ Conversely, \(A_{ij} = r_{ij} \sqrt{A_{ii} A_{jj}}\) (Henderson 1976). This is what stats::cov2cor() computes from the additive relationship matrix. Being a correlation, it lies between 0 and 1 (the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality guarantees that \(A_{ij} \le \sqrt{A_{ii} A_{jj}}\)), and every individual has a relationship of 1 with itself.

Its interpretation follows: it measures how similar two individuals are compared with how similar an individual is to itself. A value of 1 means that two individuals are as similar as an individual is to itself, as with members of a line selfed for many generations; a value of 0.5 means that they are half as similar. It does not remove the effect of inbreeding on resemblance, it measures resemblance against that reference, which is why it stays between 0 and 1 whatever the inbreeding. In the selfing example above, the two offspring have \(A = 1.5\) but \(r = 1.5 / 1.75 \approx 0.86\): they are 86 percent as similar to each other as each of them is to itself.

Hamilton's regression coefficient of relatedness ("hamilton")

Hamilton (1964a, b) used Wright's coefficient of relationship, in a population without inbreeding, in the first formulation of inclusive fitness. To allow for inbreeding, Hamilton (1972) then defined the regression coefficient of relatedness of a relative \(B\) to an actor \(A\) as \(b_{AB} = 2 r_{AB} / (1 + F_A)\), where \(r_{AB}\), the probability that a gene of \(A\) is present in a random gamete of \(B\), is their kinship coefficient. In his words, it "measures the regression of B's additive genotype on that of A". With inbreeding, the \(r\) of Hamilton's rule \(rb > c\) is this regression coefficient rather than a correlation. Michod and Hamilton (1980) showed that the various coefficients of relatedness proposed for Hamilton's rule are equivalent, and that they reduce, in particular when gene effects are additive, to this regression of the genotype of the recipient of a behaviour on that of the actor, $$b_{ij} = \frac{\mathrm{Cov}(g_i, g_j)}{\mathrm{Var}(g_i)} = \frac{A_{ij}}{A_{ii}} = \frac{2\phi_{ij}}{1 + F_i}$$ where \(i\) is the actor and \(j\) the recipient. In the matrix returned, rows are actors and columns are recipients: R[i, j] is the relatedness of recipient j from the point of view of actor i. The matrix is not symmetric when individuals differ in their inbreeding coefficients, which is also when the regression and the correlation (Wright's coefficient) differ (Michod and Hamilton 1980). Its values lie between 0 and 1 (see the section Range of values), and all individuals have a relatedness of 1 with themselves. Its interpretation is similar to that of Wright's coefficient, but from the point of view of the actor only: R[i, j] = 1 means that, as far as the genes of the actor i are concerned, the recipient j is as similar to i as i is to itself.

Range of values

The ranges given in the second table above all follow from one property: in a pedigree of diploid individuals, nobody is more related to another individual than to itself, $$A_{ij} \le \min(A_{ii}, A_{jj})$$ Consequently:

  • The off-diagonal values of the additive relationship are at most 2 and those of the kinship at most 1, while Wright's coefficient (the additive relationship divided by the geometric mean of the two diagonal values) and Hamilton's coefficient (divided by the diagonal value of the actor) are at most 1.

  • Without inbreeding, every diagonal value of the additive relationship is 1, so the additive relationship between two individuals is then at most 1, the value for identical twins or clones.

  • Values of the additive relationship above 1 therefore only occur with inbreeding. For example, after n generations of selfing the inbreeding coefficient is 1 - (1/2)^n, so the diagonal is 1.5, 1.75, 1.875, ... The maximum of 2 (a kinship of 1) is approached but never reached, since founders are assumed not to be inbred.

Here is why the property \(A_{ij} \le \min(A_{ii}, A_{jj})\) holds. Take two individuals, and call \(i\) the one that is not an ancestor of the other, \(j\); let \(m\) and \(d\) be the parents of \(i\), so that \(A_{ij} = (A_{mj} + A_{dj})/2\) and \(A_{ii} = 1 + A_{md}/2\).

  • Draw one allele at random from each of \(j\), \(m\) and \(d\). If the allele of \(j\) is identical by descent both with that of \(m\) and with that of \(d\), then these two are identical by descent with each other. In terms of probabilities, \(\phi_{mj} + \phi_{dj} \le 1 + \phi_{md}\), i.e. \(A_{mj} + A_{dj} \le 2 + A_{md}\), which is \(A_{ij} \le A_{ii}\).

  • \(A_{ij}\) is the mean of \(A_{mj}\) and \(A_{dj}\). If neither exceeds \(A_{jj}\), their mean does not either. As \(m\) and \(d\) come before \(i\) in the pedigree, the result follows step by step from the founders, which are related to nobody but themselves.

An unknown parent counts as a founder that appears nowhere else in the pedigree, so the same reasoning applies.

Assumptions

Whatever the measure, founders (individuals with unknown parents) are assumed to be unrelated to each other and not inbred, an unknown parent is treated as unrelated to everybody, and only autosomal loci are considered. All values are therefore relative to the founders of the pedigree.

See also

fastrel_ped(), fastrel_vec() and rel_get(), which take the argument metric.

Examples

## G is a founder; P is obtained by selfing G; O1 and O2 by selfing P
ped <- data.frame(id  = c("G", "P", "O1", "O2"),
                  dad = c(NA, "G", "P", "P"),
                  mom = c(NA, "G", "P", "P"))
fastrel_ped(ped)                       # additive relationship, the default
#>    G   P   O1   O2
#> G  1 1.0 1.00 1.00
#> P  1 1.5 1.50 1.50
#> O1 1 1.5 1.75 1.50
#> O2 1 1.5 1.50 1.75
fastrel_ped(ped, metric = "kinship")   # probabilities
#>      G    P    O1    O2
#> G  0.5 0.50 0.500 0.500
#> P  0.5 0.75 0.750 0.750
#> O1 0.5 0.75 0.875 0.750
#> O2 0.5 0.75 0.750 0.875
fastrel_ped(ped, metric = "wright")    # correlations
#>            G         P        O1        O2
#> G  1.0000000 0.8164966 0.7559289 0.7559289
#> P  0.8164966 1.0000000 0.9258201 0.9258201
#> O1 0.7559289 0.9258201 1.0000000 0.8571429
#> O2 0.7559289 0.9258201 0.8571429 1.0000000
fastrel_ped(ped, metric = "hamilton")  # regressions: row = actor
#>            G         P        O1        O2
#> G  1.0000000 1.0000000 1.0000000 1.0000000
#> P  0.6666667 1.0000000 1.0000000 1.0000000
#> O1 0.5714286 0.8571429 1.0000000 0.8571429
#> O2 0.5714286 0.8571429 0.8571429 1.0000000

## the conversions from the additive relationship matrix
A <- fastrel_ped(ped)
all.equal(fastrel_ped(ped, metric = "kinship"), A / 2)
#> [1] TRUE
all.equal(fastrel_ped(ped, metric = "wright"), cov2cor(A))
#> [1] TRUE
all.equal(fastrel_ped(ped, metric = "hamilton"), A / diag(A))
#> [1] TRUE

## without inbreeding, all but the kinship are the same
ped2 <- data.frame(id = c("a", "b", "c", "d"), dad = c(NA, NA, "b", "b"),
                   mom = c(NA, NA, "a", "a"))
all.equal(fastrel_ped(ped2), fastrel_ped(ped2, metric = "wright"))
#> [1] TRUE
all.equal(fastrel_ped(ped2), fastrel_ped(ped2, metric = "hamilton"))
#> [1] TRUE
